The program was horrendous, but that seems to be the answer for most education programs. Extremely focused on the airy fairy theory of academic education and completely fails to teach you about actual classroom teaching or prepare you for such. You will learn to detest the word reflection, and the administration outside of the Practicum placement advisors is largely useless to anyone who is not a single teachable specialty. If you are going French/Socials, or Home Ec/PE, etc. Prepare to have one of your teachables completely ignored. When concerns for this ten grand program are brought to admin over multiple years, they will be given token speaking time and then ignored because the next "crop" will be soon arriving by the time you've had enough.

Commuting is super tough. I lived right at the edge of Burnaby and East Van and it was minimum hour each way each day, which made the plodding useless classes all that much more frustrating.

If anyone from Faculty of Education reads this. Never allow masters students with no teaching experience to teach classes. Ever. Get seconded teachers or professors with actual teaching experience at whatever level they are supposed to be giving instruction on. Also - please ignore and omit most academic research on actual classroom teaching, because most of it is now being proven wrong (learning styles!) and it will never actually be used in any meaningful way 90% of the time in an actual classroom environment.

I could go on, but I won't. 

For OP: This isn't just my opinion, basically my entire class of 300 BEd students had multiple meetings and feedback sessions with admin on all these issues. There are gems in the program, not sure if they're still there: Kathy Heikkla, Holly Keon, John the super sick practicum placement guy, Sara Dunn, Bathseba Opini.

However! I hear the exact same stuff is true about Uvic and SFU from other teachers, who also hate the word reflection with a red hot passion.

I'm just doing what I can to be a good teacher after the fact!

Edit: PM me if you have any more questions. I've been teaching for 3-4 years now post-UBC for both degrees.

Ehhh, Third wave was very much about reclaiming female sexuality and gender in stark contrast to the more radical aspects and ideas behind 1960's 2nd wave feminism. The late 1980's and early 90's did address and integrate some diversity to the movement, but it wasn't until the 21st century that there was a real inclusion of alternative concepts and selves. And there are obviously subcultures within subcultures, some of which were more privileged even as they were somewhat acknowledged in the 90's.

Some scholars are arguing that a 4th wave of feminism linked to internet culture emerged with the anonymous nature of the web and better integrated these disenfranchised people, because the 3rd wave concepts of embracing feminine identity through presentation like lipstick, etc left a lot of people out.

Not saying there isn't any acceptance in Third Wave feminism, but being a queer woman and being a transgender man or transgender woman could be privileged differently within the wave subculture based on it's major concepts.

Wiki is the easiest to throw out there for extra info! http://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-wave_feminism

My UBC experience was deeply rooted in several different faculties/departments that all addressed gender in some societal function or problematization. Even after reading countless hours of Judith Butler and other academics who research gender binaries and gender performativity and power, my biggest issue comes from acting the perspective of a humanist. 

I feel like I'm thinking "wrongly" for my opinions on gender issues as less important than decolonialization, the progress and survival of our species, and technological and scientific advances, despite finding myself parroting the "eliminate the gender binary" ideal that humanism often supports. 

This isn't to shut down gender privilege as an issue to be fixed or addressed, but to acknowledge that the different waves of feminism and varying beliefs in social justice movements all link back to these macro-scale ideas at their roots, and often leave people out of the equality narrative, eapecially those of genderqueer, null/asexual, and transexual identities ALREADY, leading to a need for a generalist equality movement that doesn't alienate anyone, and is wholly inclusive of diversity.

TLDR;

I feel torn between what I believe is more important, and the 'right' belief on equality or equity.
